# Introduction {#sec-intro}

According to Gallup, 22% of American workers worried technology would make their job obsolete in 2023, up 7% from 2021 [@Gallup2023]. Concerns about automation were evident years earlier. As a similary survey in 2017 by the Pew Research Center reported that 72% of Americans surveyed perceived technology as a threat because of its potential to perform many jobs currently done by humans [@Pew2017]. Central to these concerns is automation, whereby technology performs tasks previously carried out by human workers. These concerns may partly reflect the potential negative economic effects of automation, as prior studies have documented substantial losses associated with job displacement [@CouchPlaczek2010].

Evidence from prior research supports this possibility finding that displaced worker's earnings fell by more than 30% from 1993 to 2004, remaing, on average, 15% below prior earnings over the next six years[@CozziFella2016]. Local prices may shape the purchasing power associated with these earnings losses. As demonstrated by @Moretti2013, the same income can support different living standards across U.S. cities. These differences in local purchasing power make geographic scale central to the analysis, as wages or income alone can obscure meaningful differences in economic well being across places.[@Curran2006].

Examining wheter automation risk was associated with local economic conditions, we first needed a measurable indicator of vulnerability to automation. Autor’s task based framework provided the basis for this measure through the tasks performed in local labor markets. @Autor2003 first demonstrated that computers replaced routine tasks while complementing non-routine ones, which made it possible to identify work more susceptible to automation. @AcemogluAutor2011 later expanded the framework by treating tasks as the production unit and different skill groups as their suppliers. @AutorDorn2013 then applied the framework to local labor markets, finding that areas concentrated in routine work experienced employment polarization.

Nevertheless, these investigations generally examined wages and employment at geographic scales broader than the county. For our study, automation risk is measured through the task composition of county employment, while purchasing power is defined as household income adjusted for differences in local price levels. Unlike wages, which describe what a job pays, purchasing power reflects what that income can buy. We therefore investigate whether county task composition is associated with household purchasing power.

In addition, our analysis used a county level panel from 2008 to 2023, excluding 2020, with 11,983 observations across 840 counties. These counties represented approximately 84% of the U.S. population [@census_popest2023]. County employment was organized into four task groups based on the task based framework to capture differences in the types of work performed across local economies. Therfore, purchasing power was the primary outcome, while poverty, unemployment, population, and county task group shares acted as explanatory factors.

Our analysis first examined how purchasing power varied with county task group shares, poverty, unemployment, and population. A regression model was then used to test whether county task groups remained associated with purchasing power after accounting for poverty, unemployment, and population. Year indicators accounted for economic changes shared across counties in a given year, while standard errors were clustered by county for statistical inference. Diagnostic checks favored a log specification, while random forest and neural network models assessed whether nonlinear relationships captured patterns missed by the regression model. The most notable finding was that a 1% shift from non-routine cognitive to non-routine manual work was associated with approximately \$846 less purchasing power at the panel mean (95% confidence interval, ±\$38). Task groups remained associated with purchasing power after accounting for poverty and unemployment. Taken together, these results suggest that considering local purchasing power can help policymakers and economic development agencies distinguish between counties that appear similar on conventional indicators but differ in resident's economic well being.
